questions.q: What is the real migration risk this lesson identifies, more than raw data volume?
options: The three source systems have different grains and different keys, decided independently by different teams with no coordination
None of the three source systems have any usable primary keys at all
The legacy SQL Server system uses more storage than the other two combined
The CRM system cannot export data in any batch format
questions.explain: The order system's yearly-resetting order_id, the CRM's globally-unique customer_guid, and the inventory system's vendor-specific SKU format were never designed to agree.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the customer_crosswalk table?
options: It resolves three inconsistent customer references into one conformed customer key that every fact table in the new warehouse depends on
It stores a backup copy of the legacy order system in case of data loss
It replaces the need for a star schema in the new warehouse
It is a temporary table deleted immediately after the first data load
questions.explain: The crosswalk maps the legacy order system's text names and the CRM's customer_guid into one conformed_customer_key, and is described as the single most important artifact in the migration.

questions.q: Why does this migration plan move customers first, inventory in parallel, and orders last?
options: The order is set by dependency — customers are referenced by everything else, inventory is independent, and orders depend on both being correct first
The order is set alphabetically by source system name
Orders must always migrate first in any warehouse migration
The order was chosen randomly since dependency doesn't affect migration planning
questions.explain: Orders has the most dependencies on the other two sources being correct, so it migrates last, not first.

questions.q: What does the reconciliation check compare, and when is cutover approved?
options: It compares nightly totals (e.g. sum of order_total) between the legacy system and the new warehouse; cutover is approved only after reconciliation holds clean for a full business cycle
It compares CPU usage between the legacy system and the new warehouse
Cutover is approved immediately once the first day's totals match
Reconciliation is optional and skipped if the migration team is confident
questions.explain: Both old and new systems run in parallel with nightly total comparisons, and only a full business cycle (including month-end) of clean reconciliation triggers cutover.

questions.q: How does this lesson's grain assessment relate to Lesson 8's grain-first principle?
options: It applies the same grain-first thinking to existing schemas that were already fixed by three separate teams, rather than to a single new design
Grain doesn't matter when consolidating existing systems, only when designing new ones
Lesson 8's grain principle only applies to streaming systems, not batch migrations
This lesson replaces grain-first thinking with a purely volume-based assessment
questions.explain: Each source's grain and key were fixed independently long ago; this lesson applies grain-first assessment retroactively to find where those choices conflict.
